canonical_question: Is the negative enthalpy of mixing (-7 KJ/mol) sufficient to guarantee Cr2Ta formation over other possible intermetallics like CrTa or Cr3Ta2?

question_variants.question: Is the negative enthalpy of mixing (-7 KJ/mol) sufficient to guarantee Cr2Ta formation over other possible intermetallics like CrTa or Cr3Ta2?
question_variants.resolution_summary: The text provides the enthalpy of mixing value (-7 KJ/mol) for Cr and Ta, but does not contain information sufficient to determine if this value is 'sufficient' to guarantee the formation of Cr2Ta over CrTa or Cr3Ta2. The text does not provide thermodynamic calculations or phase diagrams comparing these specific intermetallics.

answers.answer: The text states the enthalpy of mixing between Cr and Ta is -7 KJ/mol, but does not provide comparative data for CrTa or Cr3Ta2 to determine if this value guarantees Cr2Ta formation.
answers.boundary_limitation: No thermodynamic comparison with other intermetallics (CrTa, Cr3Ta2) provided.
evidence_spans: Previous studies focused on mechanical properties at high- and room-temperatures, but with little research and analysis on high-temperature oxidation resistance [ [7] , [8] , [9] ].

The research shows that adding the proper amount of Al, Cr, and Si elements into the refractory high-entropy alloy can form a dense oxidation film on the surface of the alloy in a high-temperature environment, thus improving the high-temperature oxidation resistance [ [10] , [11] , [12] , [13] ].
Unfortunately, elements Al, Cr, and Si very easily form brittle intermetallic compounds with other refractory elements, resulting in reduced mechanical properties of RHEAs [ [14] , [15] , [16] ].
